blocks.text:
Fiber’s link to sleep may be due to its effect on blood sugar, said ⟦1⟧, a registered dietitian who focuses on sleep support.

“When you include fiber-rich foods at dinner or as part of a bedtime snack, you slow down glucose absorption, which can prevent middle-of-the-night blood sugar drops,” Meyer explained.

When those drops happen, the body does not just wait them out. Instead, a blood sugar drop triggers adrenaline and cortisol as a survival response. That can lead to a faster heart rate, night sweats, and hunger pangs that interrupt your sleep, Meyer said.

Fiber-rich foods may also affect sleep through the gut microbiome. When gut bacteria break down fiber, they make short-chain fatty acids [small acids made by gut bacteria], which may help control nervous system processes involved in sleep.2
Experts said fiber may be a reasonable, low-risk step that could support better sleep. But you shouldn’t treat it as a fix for poor sleep based on this study alone.

items.title: What we’re talking about
items.text: New research says a diet with lots of different plant foods and more fiber may help you sleep more deeply.

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Deep sleep is the most physically restorative part of the sleep cycle.

items.title: What you can do
items.text: Try to include a mix of plant foods and aim for around 25 to 38 grams of fiber a day. That may help with sleep and with other parts of health.

blocks.text:
What you eat during the day may do more than fuel your body—it could also affect how well you sleep that night.

A recent study published in Nature Health⟦1⟧ found that higher fiber intake was linked to a small but measurable increase in time spent in deep sleep, the most physically restorative sleep stage.

The finding does not show that fiber alone fixes sleep, but it adds to more research suggesting that diet may play an important role in sleep.

Previous research has linked diets rich in fiber and ⟦1⟧ with better sleep, the researchers noted. However, they said most studies haven’t objectively measured sleep stages or accounted for other differences that might influence both diet and sleep.

The new study aimed to do both. Nearly 3,600 predominantly healthy adults logged their meals in real time through a mobile app and wore devices capable of distinguishing among sleep stages. The participants, whose average age was 53, were split roughly evenly between men and women. Altogether, they contributed 4,793 days of dietary and sleep data—the equivalent of about 13 years.

The researchers then examined how day-to-day changes in diet related to sleep hours later, while accounting for what the person had eaten and how they had slept the previous day.

They found that eating a greater variety of plant foods was associated with a lower nighttime heart rate. Meal timing also appeared to matter: Higher-calorie evening meals were linked to more sleep but a higher heart rate, while earlier dinners were associated with shorter sleep but healthier regulation of heart rate.

One of the clearest associations involved fiber—although the differences were small. Eating more fiber relative to total calorie intake was associated with 0.59 percentage points more time spent in deep sleep and 0.76 percentage points more in ⟦2⟧, which plays an important role in brain health and function.

Notably, 25 of the 32 dietary factors studied—including carbohydrates, protein, and fat—weren’t consistently linked to sleep.

Keep in mind, however, that the study doesn’t prove that eating more fiber and a variety of plant foods directly improves sleep. Although the study’s design helped limit the influence of other variables that could affect the results, it couldn’t rule them out entirely. Randomized trials are needed to determine whether dietary changes can actually improve sleep—and who might benefit the most.

Fiber may help with sleep because it can affect blood sugar, said ⟦1⟧, a registered dietitian who focuses on sleep support.

Meyer said that fiber-rich foods at dinner or in a bedtime snack slow how fast glucose is absorbed. That can help prevent blood sugar drops in the middle of the night.

If those drops happen, the body does not just wait them out. Instead, the drop can trigger adrenaline and cortisol as a survival response. That may lead to a faster heart rate, night sweats, and hunger pangs that wake you up.

Fiber-rich foods may also affect sleep through the gut microbiome. When gut bacteria break down fiber, they make short-chain fatty acids. These may help control nervous system processes involved in sleep.

Experts said not to treat fiber as a cure for bad sleep based on the study alone. Still, eating more fiber may be a low-risk step that could support better sleep.

The research does not say how much fiber you need for a possible sleep benefit. Current guidelines say adults should aim for about 25 to 38 grams per day, depending on age and sex.

Good sources include vegetables, fruits, legumes, and whole grains. The study suggests that eating a mix of these foods may help sleep even more.

Beyond possible sleep benefits, there are other reasons to eat more high-fiber foods. Fiber supports healthy digestion, feeds helpful gut bacteria, helps you feel full between meals, and supports healthy blood sugar and cholesterol levels. That is why it is an important part of a balanced diet, no matter how it affects sleep, said dietitian ⟦2⟧.
